proposedTopics.title: Foundry
proposedTopics.description: Foundry (forge/cast/anvil/chisel) is the primary toolchain for this curriculum: Solidity-native tests, fuzzing, invariants, scripting, and gas/coverage tooling, all without leaving Solidity.

proposedTopics.title: Foundry project anatomy
proposedTopics.description: forge init scaffolds src/ (contracts), test/ (.t.sol tests), lib/ (dependencies), and script/ (deploy/interaction scripts); foundry.toml declares which directories those are and out/ holds compiled artifacts (ABI + bytecode) while cache/ holds the compiler cache. Every other Foundry feature — remappings, profiles, gas snapshots — hooks into this layout, so knowing it is the entry point to the whole tool.

proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in web3-practice (already scaffolded), confirm the src/test/lib/script/out/cache layout matches foundry.toml's src/test/script/out/libs/cache_path keys and write contracts/phase03/anatomy.md listing each directory's purpose. Done when: `forge build` succeeds and anatomy.md maps every listed foundry.toml path key to its directory. Early bootstrap: use this small setup during Phase 1 before any Solidity lab. Get the supplied sample test running and record the Foundry/Solidity versions; explain advanced contract semantics in the later language lessons, not as a setup prerequisite.

proposedTopics.description: cast is Foundry's terminal tool for reading and writing chain state without writing a script: call/send/balance/storage/logs/abi-encode against any RPC. It's the fastest way to sanity-check a deployed contract or decode a transaction.

proposedTopics.title: chisel: Solidity REPL
proposedTopics.description: chisel is an interactive Solidity shell: type an expression or statement and see its result immediately, with access to Foundry cheatcodes — faster than a full build/test cycle for checking a one-line assembly or ABI idea.

proposedTopics.title: Unit testing with forge-std
proposedTopics.description: Foundry tests are Solidity contracts inheriting forge-std's Test, using setUp() for fixtures and functions prefixed test for cases; assertions (assertEq, assertTrue, …) give readable failure diffs. Each test begins from the state created by setUp(), so one test body cannot supply state to another; with default call isolation, each top-level external call also runs in a separate transaction context.

proposedTopics.title: Cheatcodes: prank & deal
proposedTopics.description: vm.prank(addr) makes the next call appear to originate from addr (vm.startPrank/stopPrank covers a range of calls), and vm.deal(addr, amount) sets an address's ETH balance directly — together they let a test impersonate a caller and fund it without a real transfer.

requirements.purpose: Control msg.sender for one call or a bounded sequence without leaking impersonation

options.title: prank Cheatcode Reference
options.why: The canonical cheatcode page defines exactly which next call is affected and distinguishes prank from recurrent caller modification.

requirements.purpose: Set a test address balance directly without implying transfer execution

options.title: deal Cheatcode Reference
options.why: The canonical reference states the direct balance mutation used by the assertion and avoids teaching it as a real ETH transfer.

proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in test/phase03/Prank.t.sol, use vm.prank to call an onlyOwner-style function as a non-owner and assert it reverts, then vm.deal an address and assert its new balance. Done when: forge test passes and proves both the impersonation and the balance set.

proposedTopics.title: Cheatcodes: expectRevert & expectEmit
proposedTopics.description: vm.expectRevert(...) asserts the next call reverts with the expected data, and vm.expectEmit(...) compares an emitted event against the topics/data declared beforehand — both turn "it should fail/emit" into a checkable assertion instead of a try/catch.

options.title: expectEmit Cheatcode Reference

proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in test/phase03/ExpectRevertEmit.t.sol, declare an argument-free `error MyError();`, assert it with vm.expectRevert(MyError.selector), and assert an event with vm.expectEmit before a Transfer-style emit. proposedTopics.title: Fuzz testing
proposedTopics.description: A fuzz test takes typed parameters instead of none; Foundry generates a configurable number of random scenarios and reports a counterexample when the property fails. It checks a general behavior across sampled inputs instead of one hand-picked example, while vm.assume or bound keeps generated values inside the intended domain.

proposedTopics.title: Fork testing
proposedTopics.description: Fork testing runs a test against a snapshot of remote chain state (vm.createSelectFork / --fork-url), so you can call deployed contracts as they existed at a chosen block. Pinning the block number keeps that starting state reproducible across runs.

proposedTopics.title: Invariant testing
proposedTopics.description: An invariant test declares a property that must hold after randomized sequences of calls (e.g. "total shares never exceed total supply"); Foundry's fuzzer can drive a handler contract through valid multi-call histories and checks invariants after each call, catching stateful bugs that isolated examples miss.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What do src/, test/, lib/, script/, and out/ each hold in a Foundry project, and which one is safe to delete/regenerate?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: src/ = contracts, test/ = .t.sol tests, lib/ = installed dependencies, script/ = deploy/interaction scripts, out/ = compiled artifacts (ABI+bytecode), and cache/ = compiler cache. Pitfall: out/ and cache/ are generated and normally gitignored, but they are not the same directory or the same data.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Name three things cast can do without writing a Solidity script, and why cast call can never change state.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: cast call (read), cast send (write tx), cast storage (raw slot read), plus abi-encode/logs/etc. — all from the terminal against any RPC. Pitfall: cast call behaves like eth_call — it never actually mines a tx, even against a live node, so it can't be used to change state.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What makes anvil faster to iterate against than a public testnet, and what happens to its state on restart?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Instant mining, pre-funded accounts, and development RPC extensions (anvil_setBalance, snapshot/revert) make resets cheap. Pitfall: state is in memory by default; use --state (load if present, dump on exit) or the separate --load-state/--dump-state flags when persistence is intentional.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Why is chisel faster than forge test for checking a one-line Solidity/assembly idea, and what does it share with real tests?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: It evaluates each statement immediately in an interactive session instead of a full compile+run cycle, with full access to Foundry cheatcodes just like a test. Pitfall: a working chisel snippet doesn't automatically become a committed test — copy it into a real test file.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Why does each Foundry test function run against its own isolated EVM state, and what does that mean for relying on test execution order?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Every test* function gets setUp() re-run and a fresh state snapshot, so tests can't leak state into each other regardless of order. Pitfall: a test that depends on state created by an earlier test's body (not its own setUp()) will break — each test only sees its own setUp() plus its own body.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write a minimal Foundry test file skeleton testing a Counter contract's increment().
proposedPrompts.answerHint: import {Test} from "forge-std/Test.sol"; import {Counter} from "../src/Counter.sol"; contract CounterTest is Test { Counter c; function setUp() public { c = new Counter(); } function test_Increment() public { c.increment(); assertEq(c.count(), 1); } }

proposedPrompts.promptText: What's the difference between vm.prank and vm.startPrank/stopPrank, and what does vm.deal NOT do?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: prank affects only the next external call; startPrank/stopPrank affects every call until stopPrank. vm.deal sets a balance directly — it runs no real transfer logic (no receive/fallback triggered). Pitfall: forgetting stopPrank leaves impersonation active for later, unrelated calls in the same test.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write cheatcode calls making the next call appear from address(0xBEEF) with a 10 ether balance.
Where must vm.expectRevert/vm.expectEmit be placed relative to the call they check, and what's the risk of a bare vm.expectRevert() with no arguments?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Immediately before the call being tested — the cheatcode applies only to the very next external call. Pitfall: vm.expectRevert() with no args matches ANY revert reason, which can hide a wrong-reason bug — pass the specific selector/string when you can.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What do vm.warp and vm.roll each control, and does setting one automatically advance the other?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: vm.warp(ts) sets block.timestamp; vm.roll(n) sets block.number — instantly, for all subsequent calls in the test. Pitfall: warping doesn't advance block.number and vice versa; a contract checking both may need both cheatcodes set consistently.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What does Foundry do when a fuzz test fails, and why does fuzzing catch bugs example-based unit tests often miss?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: It reports the failing calldata and arguments as a counterexample. Fuzzing samples many typed inputs instead of the few a human thinks to write. Pitfall: constrain the intended domain with bound() or vm.assume(); excessive assumptions discard runs and can exhaust the rejection limit.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write a fuzz test asserting a Vault's deposit always credits the exact amount deposited.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: function testFuzz_Deposit(uint96 amount) public { vm.assume(amount > 0); vault.deposit{value: amount}(); assertEq(vault.balanceOf(address(this)), amount); }

proposedPrompts.promptText: Why does pinning a fork to a specific block number matter for test determinism?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Without a pinned block, forking 'latest' means the exact state (balances, oracle prices) differs run to run, so a passing test today could fail tomorrow for reasons unrelated to your code. Pitfall: forking without a rate-limit-safe RPC can hit limits mid-suite — use a dedicated fork RPC or cache.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What is a 'handler' in Foundry invariant testing, and what does it catch that a single fuzz test doesn't?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: A handler wraps the target's functions with bounded/valid inputs; the fuzzer calls handler functions in random sequences and order, then checks the invariant after each — catching bugs that only surface after a specific multi-call history. Pitfall: an unconstrained handler wastes runs on reverting calls — bound inputs inside the handler, not just the invariant.
